lesson.title: Macroevolution: Patterns Written in Deep Time
lesson.summary: Macroevolution describes large scale evolutionary patterns above the species level, such as the origin of new species, extinction, and long term trends in diversity, tracked across geological time.
lesson.body:
Earlier you learned how speciation happens: populations become reproductively isolated and diverge into separate species. Macroevolution is what you get when you zoom out from single speciation events and look at the accumulated pattern across millions of years and thousands of lineages. It is not a separate mechanism from the evolutionary processes you already know (mutation, natural selection, genetic drift, speciation). Rather, macroevolution is the large scale record that those same processes leave behind when you look at deep time instead of a handful of generations.

Because macroevolution builds directly on speciation, it helps to think of it as speciation events repeated and accumulated over long stretches of geologic time. A single speciation event splits one lineage into two. Do that repeatedly across a group's history, prune some branches through extinction, and let millions of years pass, and you get the sweeping patterns macroevolution studies: the rise and diversification of major groups, long term trends in body size or complexity, and the disappearance of others.

One especially clear macroevolutionary pattern is adaptive radiation, the relatively rapid diversification of a single ancestral lineage into many descendant species that fill different ecological roles. This tends to happen when a lineage reaches a new environment with few competitors, or when a mass extinction or other event clears out competitors and opens up ecological opportunities. A classic example is Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands, where a single ancestral finch population diversified into multiple species with beak shapes suited to different food sources, from crushing seeds to probing for insects. Adaptive radiation shows macroevolution in action: many separate speciation events, driven by the same underlying evolutionary mechanisms, converging into a recognizable large scale pattern.

Cladograms are central tools for studying macroevolution because they let biologists reconstruct which lineages are related, in what order they branched, and, when combined with molecular clock estimates, roughly when those branches split. Fossil evidence supplies the other half of the picture, since it is often the only direct record of extinct branches that left no living descendants.

It is worth being honest about the limits here. The fossil record is incomplete, and reconstructing macroevolutionary history always involves inference from indirect evidence. There is also ongoing discussion among biologists about the pace at which macroevolutionary change happens, whether it proceeds gradually and steadily or whether it is concentrated in shorter bursts separated by long periods of relative stability (an idea known as punctuated equilibrium). Both views agree on the underlying mechanisms of evolution; the disagreement is about tempo, and it remains an active area of paleontological research rather than a settled question.
